newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Shabans say it's too late for Zaire's Mobutu.
newsitem.headline: Shabans say it's too late for Zaire's Mobutu.

text.p: People in Zaire's second city Lubumbashi, capital of the autonomy-hungry mining province of Shaba, say President Mobutu Sese Seko's homecoming is a waste of time and look forward to his downfall.
Likening the ailing leader bluntly to a spent battery or a frozen corpse, they say they are looking to Laurent Kabila and his rebels to end three decades of hardship under Mobutu.

"He must step down immediately. It is too late for him now, after all the abuse he has put us through," said Flori Kazadi, 37, a money changer in the city which lies 2,000 km (1,200 miles) southeast of Kinshasa.

Scenting the chance that their copper-rich Shaba province might finally grasp the autonomy it has fought in vain for many times, most residents wait with open arms for Kabila and a hoped-for new order.

Kazadi and his colleagues said Mobutu, who has resided in a Swiss hotel and his French riviera villa since cancer surgery in August, blew his final chance to agree to real change on his last visit home to Kinshasa in December.
Then, three months into Kabila's rebellion which many saw as a foreign invasion, he was greeted by cheering crowds.

They thought he had come to make peace with popular leader Etienne Tshisekedi whose opposition campaigning had forced Mobutu to pay lip service in 1990 to a transition to democracy, but their hopes were dashed.
"We have had the longest transition in the history of the world," said Djo Muyanfwa, 42. "Mobutu is a dead battery."
"He's a frozen corpse," Kazadi said. A waiter in the Mokador Cafe in the centre of the whitewashed city then butted in in English: "He must go away, that crazy crook president."
Assani Mandevu, a sociology student aged 31, raised a lone voice against the resignation of the man who took power in 1965 -- the year he was born. His motives were not friendly.
"I hope that Mobutu does not resign or die. I want him to see the rebels take power by force and watch what a good job they do of running the country he has ruined," he said.
Security police, who in years gone by would have clamped down on such talk, sat scowling nearby but did not move. No one expects the Zairean army to resist Kabila if he comes here.
Kazadi said Mobutu might still have some role to play in smoothing the path to rapid elections and a change of power.
He said he hoped the former military leader would return to the impoverished, chaotic central African country the vast riches many accuse him of plundering.

Kabila comes from Shaba but it was Tshisekedi who was the favourite choice to succeed Mobutu. His party says it has sent envoys to talk to Kabila's rebels who have overrun eastern Zaire and are advancing on Lubumbashi.
"He's been fighting for years and it is the opposition who gave Kabila the courage to get as far as he has," Muyanfwa said. "We don't really know what Kabila stands for yet."

Kabila fought in unsuccessful attempts in the 1960s to win independence for Shaba, then known as Katanga, after Belgium left the Congo. He has been in relative obscurity in exile for most of the time since then.
